subject: math
title: Grade 7 Circle Graphs
seo_title: Grade 7 Circle Graphs Worksheets: Percents, Sector Angles and Conclusions (Free, with Answer Key, BC Curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 math worksheets on circle graphs for the BC curriculum: read sectors in percents, find amounts like 25% of 80 students, change percents to sector angles, make a circle graph from a table and draw conclusions. 100 questions with an answer key, good FSA practice.
key_big: A circle graph shows parts of one whole: the percents add to 100% and the angles add to 360°.
key_sub: Sector angle = percent × 360°, so 25% is 90°, not 25°. Number of people = percent × total, so 25% of 80 students is 20 students.
body_html:
A circle graph shows parts of a whole

A circle graph (also called a pie chart) splits one whole into sectors. Each sector shows a percent of the total. All the sectors add up to 100%.

Example 1

How many of the 80 students take the bus?

25% = 14. 80 ÷ 4 = 20. (Or 0.25 × 80 = 20.)

Answer: 20 students

Example 2

30% of the students in a survey chose hiking. That is 12 students. How many students were asked?

30% is 12, so 10% is 12 ÷ 3 = 4. 100% is 10 × 4 = 40.

Answer: 40 students

Sector angles

The angles at the centre add up to 360°. To find a sector angle, multiply the percent by 360°: 25% × 360° = 0.25 × 360° = 90°. So 1% is 3.6°.

Make a circle graph from a table

1. Find the total. 2. Find each percent (count ÷ total). 3. Find each angle (percent × 360°, or 360° ÷ total for each person). 4. Check: the percents add to 100% and the angles add to 360°. 5. Draw each angle with a protractor, give the graph a title and label each sector.

Choose the right graph

Use a circle graph when the data are parts of one whole: how a class gets to school, how a day or a budget is spent. Use a line graph for change over time, and a bar graph to compare amounts that are not parts of a whole. When two circle graphs have different totals, a bigger sector does not always mean more people: 25% of 400 = 100, and 40% of 250 = 100.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Drawing 25% as 25°Multiply by 3.6: 25% × 360° = 90°
Sectors that add up to 105% or 350°Check the totals: 100% and 360°
Reading 25% as 25 studentsFind 25% of the total: 25% of 80 = 20
Using 100 instead of 360 for anglesAngles add to 360°; percents add to 100%
Saying a bigger sector always means more peopleWork out the numbers when the totals are different

faq.q: How do you make a circle graph in Grade 7?
faq.a: Find the total, change each count to a percent, then multiply each percent by 360° to get the sector angle. Check that the percents add to 100% and the angles add to 360°, then draw the angles with a protractor.

faq.q: How do you find the angle of a sector from a percent?
faq.a: Multiply the percent by 360°. For example, 25% × 360° = 0.25 × 360° = 90°, so a 25% sector is a right angle, not 25°.

faq.q: How do you find the number of people from a circle graph?
faq.a: Find the percent of the total. If 25% of 80 students take the bus, 0.25 × 80 = 20 students take the bus.

faq.q: Are circle graphs on the Grade 7 FSA?
faq.a: Circle graphs are part of the BC Grade 7 math curriculum, and the Grade 7 FSA numeracy section asks students to read and use data. Reading percents, finding amounts and drawing conclusions from graphs is good FSA practice.

sets.title: Read a circle graph in percents

items.q: What percent of the students take the bus?
items.e: Read the label on the Bus sector: 25%.

items.q: Which way of getting to school is used by the most students?
items.e: The biggest sector has the biggest percent: Walk is 35%, more than Car (30%).

items.q: What percent of the students do not walk to school?
What percent of the students take the bus or ride a bike?
items.e: Add the two sectors: 25% + 10% = 35%.

items.q: What percent of the students chose spring?
items.e: The sectors add up to 100%. 45% + 25% + 20% = 90%. 100% − 90% = 10%. (270 comes from 360 − 90: percents add up to 100, not 360.)

items.q: What percent of the students chose basketball?
items.e: 30% + 25% + 15% + 10% = 80%. The whole circle is 100%, so basketball is 100% − 80% = 20%.

items.q: Which two subjects together make exactly half of the circle graph?
items.e: Half is 50%. Math 20% + Science 30% = 50%. PE and Art = 40%, Science and PE = 55%, Math and PE = 45%.

items.q: Which subject was chosen by one-quarter of the students?
items.e: One-quarter is 25%. The PE sector is 25%.

items.q: Which sector is 110 of the circle graph?
items.e: 110 = 10%. The Music sector is 10%.

items.q: How many percent more students chose apples than grapes?
items.e: Subtract: 40% − 15% = 25%. (55% adds the two sectors.)

items.q: What fraction of the students chose apples?
items.e: 40% = 40100 = 25. (140 reads the percent as a denominator.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: Grapes is the second biggest sector
Half of the students chose berries
Apples and berries are less than half
Twice as many chose apples as bananas
items.e: Apples 40% is 2 × 20% (bananas). Berries is 25%, not 50%. Apples and berries are 65%, more than half.

items.q: What percent of the recycling is food scraps?
Owen made a circle graph: hockey 40%, soccer 35%, lacrosse 30%. What is wrong?
items.e: 40% + 35% + 30% = 105%. The sectors of a circle graph must add up to exactly 100%, so one percent is wrong.

items.q: The percents in a circle graph must add up to …
items.e: A circle graph shows one whole. The whole is 100%. (360 is the number of degrees, not the percent.)

items.q: What percent of the students have a dog or a cat?
items.e: 35% + 25% = 60%. (40% is everyone else.)

items.q: What percent of the students have a pet?
items.e: Everyone not in the No pet sector has a pet: 100% − 20% = 80%. (75% forgets the Other sector.)

items.q: Which two sectors together are the same size as the Dog sector?
items.e: Dog is 35%. No pet 20% + Fish 15% = 35%. Cat and Other = 30%, Cat and Fish = 40%, Fish and Other = 20%.

items.q: A circle graph has 4 sectors that are all the same size. What percent is each sector?
items.e: 100% ÷ 4 = 25%. (90 is the angle in degrees, not the percent.)

items.q: A circle graph has 3 sectors. Two of them are 45% and 30%. What percent is the third sector?
How many students take the bus?
items.e: 25% = 14. 14 of 80 = 80 ÷ 4 = 20 students. (25 is the percent, not the number of students.)

items.q: How many students ride a bike?
items.e: 10% of 80 = 80 ÷ 10 = 8 students.

items.q: How many students walk?
How many more students walk than ride a bike?
items.e: Walk: 36. Bike: 8. 36 − 8 = 28 students. (35 is the difference in percent, not in students.)

items.q: How many students chose granola bars?
items.e: 1% of 200 = 2. 35% = 35 × 2 = 70 students. (35 would be right only for 100 students.)

items.q: How many students chose yogurt?
How many students chose fruit or yogurt?
How many students chose lacrosse?
items.e: 10% of 60 = 6 and 5% of 60 = 3. 15% = 6 + 3 = 9 students. (4 comes from 60 ÷ 15.)

items.q: How many students chose hockey?
items.e: 25% = 14. 60 ÷ 4 = 15 students.

items.q: How many students chose soccer?
items.e: 40% = 0.4. 0.4 × 60 = 24 students. (2.4 puts the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: 24 of the 60 students in a survey chose soccer. What percent is that?
items.e: 2460 = 25 = 0.4 = 40%. (36 is the number of students who did not choose soccer.)

items.q: 18 of 40 students chose hiking. What percent of the circle graph is hiking?
items.e: 1840 = 0.45 = 45%. (55% is the rest of the circle.)

items.q: 10 students chose Science World. How many students were in the survey?
items.e: Science World is 25% = 14 of the students. If 14 is 10 students, the whole is 4 × 10 = 40 students.

items.q: In a survey, 30% of the students chose hiking. That is 12 students. How many students were in the survey?
items.e: 30% is 12 students, so 10% is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 students. 100% is 10 × 4 = 40 students.

items.q: How many students come by car?
How many students ride a bike?
items.e: 8% of 500 = 8 × 5 = 40 students.

items.q: 12.5% of the 80 students in a survey chose orcas as their favourite animal. How many students is that?
items.e: 12.5% = 18. 80 ÷ 8 = 10 students. (8 is only 10%.)

items.q: Mei’s class has 32 students. 75% of them have a library card. How many students have a library card?
items.e: 75% = 34. 32 ÷ 4 = 8, and 3 × 8 = 24 students. (8 students do not have a card.)

items.q: How much does Ji-woo spend on games each month?
items.e: 20% of $40 = 0.2 × $40 = $8. ($20 reads the percent as dollars.)

items.q: 300 students voted on a new school logo. The circle graph shows 45% voted Yes. How many students voted Yes?
All the angles at the centre of a circle graph add up to …
items.e: A circle graph is a whole circle, and a full turn is 360°. (100 is for percents.)

items.q: A sector is 25% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 25% × 360° = 0.25 × 360° = 90°. A sector of 25% is NOT 25°: it is one-quarter of the circle, a right angle.

items.q: A sector is 50% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 10% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 20% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 35% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 35% × 360° = 0.35 × 360° = 126°. (12.6° puts the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: A sector is 15% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 12.5% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 12.5% × 360° = 0.125 × 360° = 45°. Check: 12.5% is 18, and 360 ÷ 8 = 45.

items.q: A sector of a circle graph has an angle of 90°. What percent is it?
items.e: 90° ÷ 360° = 0.25 = 25%. (90% reads the degrees as a percent.)

items.q: A sector of a circle graph has an angle of 72°. What percent is it?
A sector of a circle graph has an angle of 108°. What percent is it?
A sector is 13 of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. (33 is about the percent, not the angle.)

items.q: 24 students were asked. 8 chose art. What angle should the art sector be?
items.e: Each student is 360° ÷ 24 = 15°. 8 × 15° = 120°. (Or: 13 of 360° = 120°.)

items.q: 40 students were asked. 14 have a dog. What angle should the dog sector be?
A circle graph shows 45 students. How many degrees stand for each student?
items.e: 360° ÷ 45 = 8° for each student.

items.q: What is the angle of the Car sector?
items.e: 126° + 108° + 36° = 270°. The angles add up to 360°, so 360° − 270° = 90°. (270° is the total of the other three sectors, not the Car sector.)

items.q: Which sector has an angle of 72°?
items.e: 72° ÷ 360° = 0.2 = 20%. The Skating sector is 20%. (Sledding is 36°, Snowboarding 108°, Skiing 144°.)

items.q: In a circle graph, each person is 4°. How many people does the whole graph show?
items.e: 360° ÷ 4° = 90 people. (1440 multiplies instead of dividing. 25 uses 100 instead of 360.)

items.q: A circle graph shows 60 students. The soccer sector is 150°. How many students chose soccer?
items.e: Each student is 360° ÷ 60 = 6°. 150° ÷ 6° = 25 students. (15 uses 10° for each student.)

items.q: A circle graph shows 30 students. The walk sector is 132°. How many students walk?
items.e: Each student is 360° ÷ 30 = 12°. 132° ÷ 12° = 11 students. Check: 11 × 12° = 132°.

sets.title: Make a circle graph from a table

items.q: You have a table of counts. What do you do first to make a circle graph?
items.e: First add the counts to find the total. Then find each part as a percent of the total (or 360° ÷ total for each person).

items.q: To change a percent into a sector angle, you multiply the percent by …
A table shows that 9 of 36 students chose basketball. What percent should the sector show?
items.e: 936 = 14 = 25%. (27 is the number of students who did not choose basketball.)

items.q: Favourite activity of 40 students: hiking 14, skiing 12, swimming 10, biking 4. What percent should the hiking sector show?
items.e: 1440 = 0.35 = 35%. (28 doubles 14, but 40 is not 50.)

items.q: Favourite activity of 40 students: hiking 14, skiing 12, swimming 10, biking 4. What angle should the skiing sector be?
items.e: Each student is 360° ÷ 40 = 9°. 12 × 9° = 108°. (30 is the percent. 120 uses 10° for each student.)

items.q: Favourite activity of 40 students: hiking 14, skiing 12, swimming 10, biking 4. What angle should the biking sector be?
items.e: 4 × 9° = 36°. (10 is the percent, not the angle.)

items.q: 20 students: walk 9, bus 6, car 5. Which sector angles are correct?
Walk 45%, bus 35%, car 20%. Which sector angles are correct?
items.e: Multiply each percent by 3.6°: 45 × 3.6 = 162°, 35 × 3.6 = 126°, 20 × 3.6 = 72°. They add up to 360°. (135°, 105°, 60° multiplies by 3, not 3.6.)

items.q: A table has a total of 50 students. How many degrees stand for each student?
items.e: 360° ÷ 50 = 7.2° for each student. (2 uses 100 ÷ 50.)

items.q: A table shows that 12 of 48 students chose skating. What angle should the skating sector be?
items.e: 1248 = 14. 14 of 360° = 90°. (25 is the percent.)

items.q: A table shows that 7 of 40 students chose the bus. What percent should the bus sector show?
items.e: 740 = 7 ÷ 40 = 0.175 = 17.5%. (28 multiplies 7 by 4 instead of 2.5.)

items.q: A table shows that 6 of 25 students chose art. What angle should the art sector be?
items.e: Each student is 360° ÷ 25 = 14.4°. 6 × 14.4° = 86.4°. (24 is the percent.)

items.q: Ava’s table says: soccer 45%, hockey 30%, lacrosse 20%, basketball 15%. Why can’t she make a circle graph?
items.e: 45 + 30 + 20 + 15 = 110. The sectors of a circle graph must add up to 100%, so Ava made a mistake.

items.q: Noah worked out the sector angles 150°, 120° and 80°. What is wrong?
items.e: 150 + 120 + 80 = 350. The angles of a circle graph must add up to 360°, so one angle is wrong.

items.q: How students get to school: walk 50%, bus 25%, car 25%. Which circle graph matches? Key: W = walk, B = bus, C = car.
items.e: Graph C is right. Walk 50% = 180° (half), bus and car 25% = 90° each. Graph A: uses 50° for 50% and 25° for 25%, so the sectors do not fill the circle. Graph B: swaps walk and bus. Graph D: makes every sector the same size.

items.q: 30 students: soccer 15, hockey 10, lacrosse 5. Which circle graph matches? Key: S = soccer, H = hockey, L = lacrosse.
items.e: Graph A is right. Each student is 360° ÷ 30 = 12°: soccer 15 × 12° = 180°, hockey 120°, lacrosse 60°. Graph B: swaps soccer and hockey. Graph C: uses 1° for each student, so the sectors do not fill the circle. Graph D: swaps hockey and lacrosse.

items.q: 40 students: dog 16, cat 12, fish 8, rabbit 4. Which circle graph matches? Key: D = dog, C = cat, F = fish, R = rabbit.
items.e: Graph D is right. Each student is 360° ÷ 40 = 9°: dog 144°, cat 108°, fish 72°, rabbit 36°. Graph A: swaps dog and cat. Graph B: makes every sector the same size. Graph C: uses 1° for each student, so the sectors do not fill the circle.

items.q: Walk 40%, bus 30%, car 20%, bike 10%. Which circle graph matches? Key: W = walk, B = bus, C = car, K = bike.
items.e: Graph D is right. Multiply by 3.6°: walk 144°, bus 108°, car 72°, bike 36°. Graph A: uses 40° for 40% and so on, so it fills only 100° of the circle. Graph B: swaps bus and car. Graph C: draws walk as half the circle, but 40% is less than half.

items.q: Recycling: paper 50%, organics 30%, cans 20%. Which circle graph matches? Key: P = paper, O = organics, C = cans.
items.e: Graph B is right. Paper 50% = 180°, organics 30% = 108°, cans 20% = 72°. Graph A: swaps organics and cans. Graph C: uses 50° for 50% and so on, so the sectors do not fill the circle. Graph D: makes paper less than half, but 50% is exactly half.

items.q: Kai’s camping trip day: sleep 60%, hiking 25%, games 15%. Which circle graph matches? Key: S = sleep, H = hiking, G = games.
items.e: Graph B is right. Sleep 60% × 3.6° = 216°, hiking 25% = 90°, games 15% = 54°. Graph A: swaps sleep and hiking. Graph C: makes every sector the same size. Graph D: uses 60° for 60% and so on, so the sectors do not fill the circle.

sets.title: Choose the right graph and draw conclusions

items.q: Which graph is best to show what percent of a class gets to school each way?
items.e: The ways of getting to school are parts of one whole class. A circle graph shows parts of a whole.

items.q: Which graph is best to show how the temperature in Kamloops changes over one week?
items.e: Temperature changes over time. A line graph shows how it goes up and down.

items.q: Which data can NOT be shown well in a circle graph?
c: Sports students play (can pick more than one)
items.e: If students can pick more than one sport, the percents add up to more than 100%. A circle graph needs parts of one whole.

items.q: Why is a circle graph a poor choice to show the number of salmon in the Fraser River each year?
c: Salmon are too many to count
items.e: Counts for each year are not parts of one whole. A line graph or bar graph shows how they change over time.

items.q: How many hours does Owen sleep?
items.e: 24 hours = 360°, so 1 hour = 360° ÷ 24 = 15°. Sleep: 135° ÷ 15° = 9 hours. (13.5 divides by 10.)

items.q: What percent of Owen’s day is school?
items.e: 90° ÷ 360° = 0.25 = 25%. (6 is the number of hours, and 90 is the angle.)

items.q: How many more hours does Owen sleep than spend at school?
items.e: Sleep: 135° ÷ 15° = 9 hours. School: 90° ÷ 15° = 6 hours. 9 − 6 = 3 hours. (45 is the difference in degrees.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: He is at school longer than he sleeps
He sleeps more than one-third of the day
He is at school for half the day
items.e: One-third of the day is 120°. Sleep is 135°, more than 120°. School is 90°, a quarter. Homework is 15° = 1 hour.

items.q: Which school has more students who walk?
items.e: School A: 25% of 400 = 100. School B: 40% of 250 = 100. The Walk sector is bigger at School B, but School B has fewer students.

items.q: How many more students come by car at School A than at School B?
items.e: School A: 40% of 400 = 160. School B: 30% of 250 = 75. 160 − 75 = 85 students. (10 is the difference in percent.)

items.q: Liam says, “10% ride a bike at both schools, so the same number of students bike.” Is he right?
items.e: School A: 10% of 400 = 40. School B: 10% of 250 = 25. The same percent of a different total is a different number.

items.q: How many of the visitors came on BC Ferries?
items.e: 10% of 800 = 80. 60% = 6 × 80 = 480 visitors. (320 came another way.)

items.q: Which conclusion does the graph support?
c: More than half came on BC Ferries
items.e: BC Ferries is 60%, more than 50%. Plane is 25% (a quarter), floatplane is 10%. The ferry sector is 60% × 360° = 216°, not 60°.

items.q: Jasleen earned $60 babysitting. How much does she save?
items.e: 40% of $60 = 0.4 × $60 = $24. ($2.40 puts the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: Next month she earns $80 and uses the same percents. How much is for gifts?
Three Grade 7 classes raised $1200 for the Terry Fox Run. How much did 7C raise?
In a circle graph, a 90° sector stands for 45 students. How many students does the whole graph show?
items.e: 90° is 14 of 360°. If 14 is 45 students, the whole is 4 × 45 = 180 students.

items.q: In a class of 28 students, 25% take the bus. How many students in the class do not take the bus?
items.e: 25% of 28 = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 take the bus. 28 − 7 = 21 students do not. (7 answers the wrong question.)

items.q: Which conclusion does the graph support?
c: Skiing is half of the graph
items.e: 45% + 35% = 80%. Snowboarding is 35% of 200 = 70 people, not 35. Skiing is 45%, less than half. Other is 20% × 3.6° = 72°.

items.q: How many more people ski than snowboard?
items.e: Skiing: 45% of 200 = 90. Snowboarding: 35% of 200 = 70. 90 − 70 = 20 people. (10 is the difference in percent.)
